pos: n., v. (a boundary fence; rendering Hebrew mesukah and gader)
etymology: Old English hecg, an enclosure of thorn. A hedge is a living wall — a boundary grown rather than built.
biblical_def: A hedge is a protective boundary. Satan's accusation names one: “Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?” (Job 1:10) — and the whole book proceeds from its partial removal. God plants one about His vineyard and later takes it away (Isa 5:5). Ecclesiastes warns that “whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him” (Ecc 10:8), and Ezekiel looks for a man to “make up the hedge, and stand in the gap” (Eze 22:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hedge as a thicket of thorn-bushes or small trees, planted or growing so thick as to form a fence; and figuratively, any thing that separates or defends.
webster_full: HEDGE, n. A thicket of thorn-bushes or of small trees; a fence formed of bushes or small trees.
HEDGE, v.t. To enclose with a hedge; to fence.
2. To obstruct with a hedge, or to obstruct in any manner.
scriptures: Job 1:10
Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
Isa 5:5
And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down:
Ecc 10:8
He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him.
And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none.
corruption_summary: Boundaries are experienced as restriction rather than protection, so hedges are broken for the freedom on the other side — where Ecclesiastes says the serpent waits.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 1:10 is Satan's testimony, and it is accurate: hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? The adversary's complaint is that Job is fenced, and he can see the fence though Job cannot. Believers generally have no idea how much of their peace is hedge, and discover it only when a gap is permitted — which is precisely what the rest of Job explores.

Ecclesiastes 10:8 states the risk of demolition plainly: whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him. Hedges are where serpents live, so removing an old boundary is never a neutral act of tidying. Ezekiel 22:30 gives the counter-vocation — I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land — and records that God found none, which is why the wrath came.
roots_summary: Hebrew mesukah (H4881), a hedge of thorns; gader (H1447), a wall or fence; both used of vineyard boundaries.
roots_lines: Hebrew suk (H7753) — to hedge about, fence in; Job 1:10.
Hebrew mesukah (H4881) — hedge; Isaiah 5:5, I will take away the hedge thereof.
Hebrew gader (H1447) — wall, hedge; Ecclesiastes 10:8, Ezekiel 22:30.
usage: “Hast not thou made an hedge about him” — the adversary can see the fence.
“Whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him” — boundaries are where serpents live.
“Make up the hedge, and stand in the gap” — the vocation God found no one to fill.

pos: n. (a female sheep; rendering Hebrew kibsah and rachel)
etymology: Old English eowu. The Hebrew rachel is a ewe — Jacob's wife bears the name of the animal her husband tended.
biblical_def: A ewe is a female sheep. Nathan's parable turns on one: the poor man had “one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and nourished up: and it grew up together with him, and with his children… and lay in his bosom, and was unto him as a daughter” (2Sa 12:3) — and the rich man took it. Abraham sets seven ewe lambs apart as a witness at Beersheba (Gen 21:28–30), and the psalmist notes that David was taken “from following the ewes great with young” to feed Jacob his people (Psa 78:71).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ewe as a female sheep, the female of the ovine race of animals.
webster_full: EWE, n. A female sheep; the female of the ovine race of animals.
scriptures: But the poor man had nothing, save one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and nourished up: and it grew up together with him, and with his children; it did eat of his own meat, and drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was unto him as a daughter.
And Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.
From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.
And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;
corruption_summary: Nathan's method — a story that secures the verdict before the defendant knows he is on trial — is nearly extinct in a church that prefers either confrontation or silence.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Samuel 12 is the most skilful rebuke in Scripture, and its whole force rests on the ewe lamb. Nathan does not begin with adultery or murder; he begins with a poor man, one little ewe lamb, and a rich man's guest. David's anger is genuinely kindled and his sentence is passed in full — the man that hath done this thing shall surely die — and only then does Nathan say, Thou art the man. The king convicted himself while his defences were pointed elsewhere.

Psalm 78:71 keeps the pastoral image honest about its origins. David was taken from following the ewes great with young — specifically the pregnant and nursing animals, the slowest and most demanding part of the flock. That is the apprenticeship God chose for a king, and it says something about what shepherding a people actually requires: patience with those who cannot keep up.
roots_summary: Hebrew kibsah (H3535), a ewe lamb; rachel (H7353), a ewe — the name of Jacob's wife.
roots_lines: Hebrew kibsah (H3535) — ewe lamb; 2 Samuel 12:3, Genesis 21:28.
Hebrew rachel (H7353) — ewe; Genesis 31:38, Isaiah 53:7, as a sheep before her shearers is dumb.
Hebrew ul (H5763) — to give suck; Psalm 78:71, the ewes great with young.
usage: “One little ewe lamb… was unto him as a daughter” — the story that convicted a king.
“Thou art the man” — the verdict David had already passed on himself.
“From following the ewes great with young” — a king's apprenticeship.

pos: n. (a young cow; rendering Hebrew parah and eglah)
etymology: Old English heahfore. A heifer is a cow that has not calved — young, unbroken, and in the law's usage, never yoked.
biblical_def: A heifer is a young cow. The red heifer ordinance requires one “without spot, wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke” (Num 19:2); burned outside the camp, her ashes purified the defiled. Hebrews reasons from her to Christ: if the ashes of an heifer sanctify to the purifying of the flesh, “how much more shall the blood of Christ… purge your conscience from dead works?” (Heb 9:13–14). Samson's riddle-breakers are met with “if ye had not plowed with my heifer” (Jdg 14:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a heifer as a young cow.
webster_full: HEIFER, n. A young cow.
scriptures: Num 19:2

This is the ordinance of the law which the LORD hath commanded, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring thee a red heifer without spot, wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke:
Heb 9:13
For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh:
Heb 9:14
How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
Jdg 14:18 (WEB)

The men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” He said to them, “If you hadn’t plowed with my heifer, you wouldn’t have found out my riddle.”
corruption_summary: The purification rites are skimmed as archaic hygiene, so Hebrews' central argument — how much more — loses the lesser term it is reasoning from.
corruption_paragraphs: The red heifer ordinance is deliberately strange: an unblemished animal that had never worn a yoke, killed outside the camp, wholly burned, her ashes stored and mixed with running water to cleanse anyone defiled by contact with death. Every detail points somewhere — unyoked, outside the camp, a remedy kept ready for the inevitable defilement that touching a corpse brings.

Hebrews 9 builds its argument on exactly that ritual, and the argument only works if the lesser term is granted. If the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? The heifer cleansed the body's ceremonial defilement; Christ reaches the conscience, which is the room no ash could enter.
roots_summary: Hebrew parah (H6510), a heifer, the red heifer of Numbers 19; eglah (H5697), a calf or heifer; Greek damalis (G1151) in Hebrews 9:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew parah (H6510) — heifer; Numbers 19:2, a red heifer without spot.
Hebrew eglah (H5697) — heifer, calf; Judges 14:18, Jeremiah 46:20.
Greek damalis (G1151) — heifer; only Hebrews 9:13, the ashes of an heifer.
usage: “Without spot… upon which never came yoke” — the red heifer's qualifications.
“How much more shall the blood of Christ… purge your conscience” — the argument from the lesser.
“If ye had not plowed with my heifer” — Samson on a riddle betrayed.

pos: n. (a bird of the waste places; rendering Hebrew bath yaanah and kos)
etymology: Old English ule, imitative of the call. In Scripture the owl is not wisdom's emblem but desolation's — a bird that occupies what men abandon.
biblical_def: The owl is an unclean bird of ruins. The law forbids it as food (Lev 11:16), and the prophets post it in the rubble of fallen cities: Babylon shall be a place where “owls shall dwell there” (Isa 13:21), and Edom shall be possessed by “the owl also and the raven” (Isa 34:11). The psalmist takes the image for his own loneliness: “I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert” (Psa 102:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an owl as a fowl of the genus Strix, a nocturnal bird of prey, with large head and eyes, that preys by night.
webster_full: OWL, n. A fowl of the genus Strix, that flies chiefly in the night; a nocturnal bird of prey.
OWLET, n. An owl; a young owl.
scriptures: But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there.
But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness.
I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert.
And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,
corruption_summary: Loneliness is treated as a problem to be solved or a shame to be hidden, when Psalm 102 hands the believer language for it and puts that language in the songbook.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 102 carries the superscription a prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint before the LORD — and the imagery is unsparing: I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert. I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top. The psalmist compares himself to the birds that live where nobody else will, and this is inspired prayer. Scripture does not require the desolate to sound cheerful.

The prophetic use explains the force of the comparison. Owls appear in Isaiah where cities have fallen — wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there. To call oneself an owl of the desert is to say I am living in the ruins. And the psalm that says it turns, before it ends, to the God whose years shall have no end and whose servants' children shall be established.
roots_summary: Hebrew bath yaanah (H1323/H3284), daughter of greed or of the wilderness, rendered owl or ostrich; kos (H3563), the little owl of Leviticus 11.
roots_lines: Hebrew bath yaanah — owl or ostrich; Isaiah 13:21, 34:13, Micah 1:8.
Hebrew kos (H3563) — little owl; Leviticus 11:17, Psalm 102:6.
Hebrew yanshuph (H3244) — great owl; Isaiah 34:11, Leviticus 11:17.
usage: “Owls shall dwell there” — the tenant of a fallen city.
“I am like an owl of the desert” — inspired language for desolation.
“A sparrow alone upon the house top” — the psalm's companion image.

pos: n. pl. (predators of the flock; rendering Greek lukos)
etymology: Old English wulf. In pastoral cultures the wolf needs no explanation: it is the standing threat to sheep, and Scripture uses it for nothing else.
biblical_def: Wolves are the flock's predators, and Scripture applies the word almost exclusively to false teachers. Christ warns of those who “come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15), and Paul warns the Ephesian elders that “after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock; also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things” (Act 20:29–30). The hireling flees because he sees the wolf coming (Joh 10:12), while Christ sends His own out “as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Mat 10:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a wolf as a beast of prey of the canine genus, which resembles a dog, is fierce and carnivorous, and preys on sheep.
webster_full: WOLF, n. An animal of the canine genus, a beast of prey that kills sheep and other small domestic animals.
2. Any ravenous, cruel person.
scriptures: Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
corruption_summary: Congregations expect wolves to arrive from outside and to look hostile, while Paul's warning is that they arise from among the elders and speak the flock's own dialect.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 20:30 contains the sentence that makes the danger structural rather than external: also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them. Paul is addressing ordained elders of a healthy church, and telling them the next generation of wolves is currently sitting among them. That is why he commends them to God and to the word of his grace — the safeguard is not a screening process but a standard.

John 10:12 exposes the difference between a shepherd and an employee, and it is only visible under threat. The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep. Nobody can tell them apart in fair weather; both feed, both lead, both are present. The wolf performs the audit. A minister's real relation to the flock is revealed on the day that staying costs him something.
roots_summary: Greek lukos (G3074), a wolf; harpax (G727), ravening, rapacious — the same adjective used of extortioners.
roots_lines: Greek lukos (G3074) — wolf; Matthew 7:15, 10:16, John 10:12, Acts 20:29.
Greek harpax (G727) — ravening, rapacious; Matthew 7:15, and 1 Corinthians 5:11 of extortioners.
Greek barus (G926) — grievous, heavy; Acts 20:29, grievous wolves.
usage: “In sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” — the disguise is the flock's own fabric.
“Of your own selves shall men arise” — the danger is internal.
“The hireling fleeth… and careth not for the sheep” — the wolf performs the audit.

etymology: From Latin radere, to scrape. In Scripture the razor is chiefly an instrument of vow — and, in the prophets, of judgment.
biblical_def: A razor shaves. The Nazarite vow is defined by its absence: “there shall no razor come upon his head… he shall be holy” (Num 6:5), which is why Samson's shaving broke him (Jdg 16:17). Isaiah turns the instrument into a figure of foreign invasion: “the Lord shall shave with a razor that is hired… the head, and the hair of the feet” (Isa 7:20). The psalmist describes a deceitful tongue as “like a sharp razor, working deceitfully” (Psa 52:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a razor as an instrument for shaving off beard or hair.
webster_full: RAZOR, n. An instrument for shaving off beard or hair.
2. The tusk of a boar.
scriptures: Num 6:5

All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the LORD, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow.

That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother's womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.
Isa 7:20
In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard.
Psa 52:2
Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.
corruption_summary: Samson's story is read as a lesson about hair or willpower, when the hair was only the visible term of a vow he had been dismantling for years.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 16 is often taught as though the strength lived in the hair, which makes God a magician and Samson a victim of a haircut. The narrative says otherwise: the hair was the last remaining sign of a Nazarite vow Samson had already broken at every other point — touching the carcase of the lion, feasting with the Philistines, keeping company he had been separated from. The razor did not take his strength; it published a separation that had long since gone.

Psalm 52:2 supplies the razor's other use, and the comparison is precise. Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully. A razor's danger is not that it is heavy but that it is fine: it parts skin before the cut is felt. That is exactly how slander operates, and why the psalm's subject is Doeg the Edomite, who destroyed a whole town of priests with a report.
roots_summary: Hebrew taar (H8593), a razor or knife-sheath; galach (H1548), to shave — the verb of both vow and disgrace.
roots_lines: Hebrew taar (H8593) — razor; Numbers 6:5, Judges 13:5, Isaiah 7:20, Psalm 52:2.
Hebrew galach (H1548) — to shave; Judges 16:17, 19, and of the leper's cleansing in Leviticus 14:8.
Hebrew nazir (H5139) — Nazarite, separated one; the vow the razor would break.
usage: “There shall no razor come upon his head” — the vow's visible term.
“The Lord shall shave with a razor that is hired” — invasion as a haircut.
“Like a sharp razor, working deceitfully” — the tongue that cuts before it is felt.

etymology: Needle with work — the translators' term for the embroiderer's craft, distinguished in Exodus from the weaver's and the cunning workman's.
biblical_def: Needlework is embroidery. It is named as a distinct sanctuary craft: the gate of the court was “wrought with needlework” (Exo 27:16), and Aholiab was filled with skill as “an embroiderer in blue, and in purple… and of them that do any work” (Exo 38:23). The king's daughter is brought to the King “in raiment of needlework” (Psa 45:14), and Sisera's mother imagines her son dividing spoil that includes “a prey of divers colours of needlework” (Jdg 5:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines needlework as work executed with a needle; the business of a seamstress; and style of embroidery.
webster_full: NEEDLEWORK, n. Work executed with a needle; or the business of a seamstress.
2. The art or business of embroidering.
scriptures: And for the gate of the court shall be an hanging of twenty cubits, of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, wrought with needlework: and their pillars shall be four, and their sockets four.
And with him was Aholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver, and a cunning workman, and an embroiderer in blue, and in purple, and in scarlet, and fine linen.
She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee.
Jdg 5:30

Have they not sped? have they not divided the prey; to every man a damsel or two; to Sisera a prey of divers colours, a prey of divers colours of needlework, of divers colours of needlework on both sides, meet for the necks of them that take the spoil?
corruption_summary: Craft is treated as decoration rather than calling, so the church commissions skill for its buildings and rarely honours it as the Spirit-given gift Exodus says it is.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 31 is the first place in Scripture where someone is said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and the man is a craftsman. I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship — to devise cunning works, to work in gold, in silver, in brass, and in cutting of stones. Bezaleel and Aholiab were given the Spirit for design and embroidery, which sets skilled making inside the doctrine of spiritual gifts rather than beside it.

Psalm 45:14 places needlework at the highest moment of the psalm, where the bride is brought to the King: she shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework. The New Testament picks up the figure of a church presented to Christ, and the detail is worth keeping — what is presented is not plain but worked, made beautiful by patient hands over long hours.
roots_summary: Hebrew riqmah (H7553), embroidery, variegated work; raqam (H7551), to embroider — the craft of the tabernacle's screens.
roots_lines: Hebrew riqmah (H7553) — embroidery, needlework; Psalm 45:14, Judges 5:30, Ezekiel 16:10.
Hebrew raqam (H7551) — to embroider, variegate; Exodus 26:36, 27:16, 38:23.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to devise, of the cunning workman; the higher craft of the veil's cherubim.
usage: “An hanging… wrought with needlework” — a named sanctuary craft.
“Brought unto the king in raiment of needlework” — the bride is worked, not plain.
“A prey of divers colours of needlework” — the spoil Sisera's mother imagined.

pos: n., v. (a bed, to lie down; rendering Hebrew rabats, Greek klinidion)
etymology: From French coucher, to lay down. Scripture's couch is a sickbed, a place of grief, or a lion's lair — rarely a place of ease.
biblical_def: A couch is a place of lying down. The paralytic is told to take his up and walk (Luk 5:24), and Peter's shadow falls on the sick laid on couches in the street (Act 5:15). David waters his with tears: “all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Psa 6:6). Amos condemns those who “stretch themselves upon their couches” while Joseph's ruin goes unnoticed (Amo 6:4–6), and Jacob's blessing on Judah pictures a lion that “couched as a lion” (Gen 49:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines couch as a bed; a place for rest or sleep; and as a verb, to lay down, to lie down on a place of repose.
webster_full: COUCH, n. A bed; a place for rest or sleep.
2. A layer or stratum.
COUCH, v.i. To lie down, as on a bed or place of repose.
2. To lie down, as a beast.
scriptures: Psa 6:6
I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.
Amo 6:4
That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;
Luk 5:24
But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power upon earth to forgive sins, (he said unto the sick of the palsy,) I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house.
Gen 49:9
Judah is a lion's whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up?
corruption_summary: Amos 6 indicts a comfort that is not sinful in itself — beds of ivory, music, good wine — but is damning because of what it manages not to notice.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 6:4-6 is uncomfortably specific: that lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock… that chant to the sound of the viol… that drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments. Nothing in the list is condemned as such. The indictment arrives in the last clause: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. Comfort becomes sin at the point where it purchases insensibility.

Psalm 6:6 shows the couch's other use, and it is a permission the church rarely grants. I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears. This is a king, in the songbook, describing nights of unmanaged grief. The psalm still ends in confidence, but it does not arrive there by shortening the night.
roots_summary: Hebrew rabats (H7257), to lie down, crouch; eres (H6210), a bedstead or couch; Greek klinidion (G2826), a small bed.
roots_lines: Hebrew eres (H6210) — couch, bedstead; Psalm 6:6, Amos 6:4, Deuteronomy 3:11 of Og's bedstead of iron.
Hebrew rabats (H7257) — to couch, lie down; Genesis 49:9, he couched as a lion.
Greek klinidion (G2826) — small couch, bed; Luke 5:19, 24, take up thy couch and go.
usage: “I water my couch with my tears” — a king's unmanaged grief, in the songbook.
“They are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph” — where comfort becomes sin.
“Take up thy couch, and go into thine house” — the bed carried out by the man it carried in.

pos: n. (the border of a garment; rendering Hebrew shul, Greek kraspedon)
etymology: Old English hem, a border. The hem is a garment's edge — its lowest and least honoured part, which is why the Gospels put it to such use.
biblical_def: The hem is a garment's border. The high priest's robe was hemmed with pomegranates and golden bells (Exo 28:33–34). The woman with the issue of blood reasons, “If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole”, and touches “the hem of his garment” (Mat 9:20–21); at Gennesaret the sick besought Him that they might only touch it, “and as many as touched were made perfectly whole” (Mat 14:36). Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, “and his train filled the temple” (Isa 6:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hem as the border of a garment, doubled and sewed to strengthen it and prevent the ravelling of the threads.
webster_full: HEM, n. The border of a garment, doubled and sewed to strengthen it and prevent the ravelling of the threads.
2. Edge; border.
HEM, v.t. To form a hem or border; to fold and sew down the edge.
scriptures: Mat 9:20
And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment:
And besought him that they might only touch the hem of his garment: and as many as touched were made perfectly whole.
And beneath upon the hem of it thou shalt make pomegranates of blue, and of purple, and of scarlet, round about the hem thereof; and bells of gold between them round about:
Isa 6:1
In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.
corruption_summary: The hem story is retold as a lesson about the woman's faith technique, when the Gospels emphasize the opposite — the power was in Him, and the hem was merely the nearest reachable part.
corruption_paragraphs: The detail that matters is the hem's position. A garment's border is its lowest edge, dragging near the dust, and a woman ceremonially unclean for twelve years could reach it from behind without being seen or requiring anyone to touch her. She came at Christ from the only direction her condition allowed, took hold of the least honourable part of His clothing, and was healed immediately. Nothing in the story rewards boldness; it rewards contact.

Christ's response settles the theology. He would not let the healing stay anonymous — who touched me? — and when she came trembling and told all the truth, He said, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace. The publicity was for her sake, so she left with a word and a name instead of a stolen cure. Faith that touches the hem is not a technique for extracting power; it is a person reaching a Person.
roots_summary: Hebrew shul (H7757), the skirt or hem of a robe; Greek kraspedon (G2899), border, fringe — the tassel the law required at a garment's corners.
roots_lines: Hebrew shul (H7757) — skirt, hem; Exodus 28:33-34, Isaiah 6:1, his train filled the temple.
Greek kraspedon (G2899) — hem, border, fringe; Matthew 9:20, 14:36, 23:5.
Hebrew tsitsith (H6734) — fringe; Numbers 15:38, the commanded border of blue.
usage: “Touched the hem of his garment” — the nearest reachable part.
“As many as touched were made perfectly whole” — the power was in Him.
“His train filled the temple” — the hem of the Lord's robe fills the house.

pos: n. (a small flat loaf; rendering Hebrew uggah and challah)
etymology: From Old Norse kaka. A biblical cake is not confectionery but a flat baked loaf — ordinary bread in an ordinary shape.
biblical_def: A cake is a small flat loaf. The widow of Zarephath's is the famous one: she has “an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse” and is gathering sticks to dress it for herself and her son that they may “eat it, and die” — and Elijah asks for it first: “Make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me” (1Ki 17:12–13). An angel bakes one for Elijah in the wilderness (1Ki 19:6). Hosea rebukes Ephraim as “a cake not turned” (Hos 7:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cake as a small mass of dough baked; or a composition of flour, butter, sugar or other ingredients, baked in a small mass.
webster_full: CAKE, n. A small mass of dough baked; or a composition of flour, butter, sugar, or other ingredients, baked in a small mass.
2. Something in the form of a cake, rather flat than high.
3. A mass of matter concreted.
scriptures: And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.
And Elijah said unto her, Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me, and after make for thee and for thy son.
And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again.
Hos 7:8
Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people; Ephraim is a cake not turned.
corruption_summary: Give first is preached as a formula for return, when Elijah's request to a starving widow is intelligible only as a claim on God's word, not on her prospects.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 17 is nearly offensive if the promise is removed. A prophet asks a destitute widow, preparing her last meal before she and her son starve, to feed him first. What makes it faith rather than exploitation is the sentence attached: for thus saith the LORD God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth. The claim rests on a word given, and she obeyed a promise, not a technique.

Hosea 7:8 supplies one of Scripture's sharpest images for a half-committed people: Ephraim is a cake not turned — burnt on one side, raw on the other, and useless either way. It describes a religion with real heat applied at one point and none at all elsewhere: fervent in worship and unjust in business, or orthodox in doctrine and cold in the house. The remedy is not less fire but turning.
roots_summary: Hebrew uggah (H5692), a round flat cake baked on coals; challah (H2471), a pierced cake of the offerings.
roots_lines: Hebrew uggah (H5692) — a cake baked on coals; 1 Kings 17:13, 19:6, Genesis 18:6, Hosea 7:8.
Hebrew challah (H2471) — a perforated cake of the meat offering; Leviticus 2:4, 24:5.
Hebrew qemach (H7058) — meal, flour; the handful in the widow's barrel.
usage: “Make me thereof a little cake first” — a claim on a word, not on her prospects.
“A cake baken on the coals” — the angel's provision under the juniper.
“Ephraim is a cake not turned” — burnt one side, raw the other.
